strengths: The paper presents a coherent application of learned edit-distance embeddings to codeword selection and decoding, addressing a relevant problem in DNA storage. The stated exclusion of radius-two Levenshtein neighborhoods correctly ensures minimum code distance at least three.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements over random codeword selection across ten runs. The decoding experiments provide useful initial evidence: querying four neighbors yields no failures in 100,000 sampled single-edit corruptions at each tested length.

The long-sequence experiments investigate synchronization recovery, multiple errors within segments, and outer Reed–Solomon correction. The manuscript acknowledges approximation errors and explicitly identifies its redundancy conjecture as unproved.
weaknesses: A straightforward baseline undermines the central code-construction comparison. In an independent check, lexicographic greedy selection—retain the first remaining word and exclude its radius-two neighbors—produced 311, 1,025, and 3,451 codewords for lengths 7, 8, and 9, respectively, exceeding the reported DEGS maxima of 275, 900, and 3,011. I exhaustively verified that the single-edit neighborhoods were disjoint for each constructed codebook. Comparison only against random selection therefore does not establish an advantage from learning.

Section 3.2 incorrectly claims that batch normalization forces embeddings to follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Normalizing moments does not imply Gaussianity. Consequently, Equation 6 is an unsupported modeling assumption, and the paper does not establish that its density ranking predicts the radius-two neighborhood sizes relevant to code construction. Ablations of the modified loss and alternative selection scores are also missing.

The optimality claims exceed the evidence. Agreement with a redundancy expression over lengths 7–11 establishes neither finite-length optimality nor asymptotic order-optimality. Figure 4 lacks tight cardinality bounds and comparisons with stronger finite-length constructions. The explicit conjecture is appropriately qualified, but the stronger abstract and introductory claims remain unsupported.

The decoding guarantees and complexity claims require qualification. Minimum distance three guarantees exact bounded-distance decoding, whereas the learned shortlist can omit the correct codeword; exact reranking cannot repair that omission. K-d trees do not provide unconditional logarithmic query time, and the practical decoder incurs additional exact-distance computations. Full DFS runtime, pruning behavior, construction costs, and memory usage are not evaluated. The timing comparison also omits simple exact decoding by enumerating single-edit neighbors and checking codebook membership.

Evidence for practical DNA-storage advantages is limited to approximately 150-nucleotide sequences under one independent 1% channel with equal insertion, deletion, and substitution probabilities. There are no matched comparisons with the cited practical codes or robustness studies across channel conditions. Zero observed errors after outer coding does not establish general reliability, especially without clearly specified RS block lengths, symbol layout, and post-correction block failure statistics.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the central results. The manuscript omits the concrete base loss, embedding dimension and full architecture, training-pair sampling, optimization settings, handling of variable-length inputs, and precise DFS pruning thresholds. Section 3.6 promises future code release, but the supplied description does not support faithful reproduction. Together with the stronger simple baseline and unsupported technical claims, these shortcomings outweigh the promising prototype results.
